title: Permission Groups Discovery: Cloud Groups
summary: Cloud groups discovery maps the identity layer of a tenant rather than a single host, and in cloud environments that layer is where all the power sits. An attacker holding a valid token does not need to compromise a server to learn who can do what, because the provider exposes the answer as ordinary read only interface calls. Typical queries list the directory roles and their members in Microsoft 365, list the groups a given user belongs to through the Azure command line, list group resources available to a user through the Cloud Identity interface, and in AWS list the policies attached to a role through the role policy listing calls. A related behaviour reads the access control list of a stored object to learn which other accounts and services already have access to it, which turns discovery directly into a targeting decision. The evidence is genuinely good when audit logging is enabled, because every provider records the caller identity, the action name, the target resource, the source address, and often a client user agent, so the reviewer can separate a console login from a scripted call. That is also the main detection difficulty: infrastructure as code pipelines, backup tools, and security posture products make broad listing calls continuously. The useful discriminators are a caller that has never performed enumeration before, a new or unexpected source address, a workload identity calling identity management interfaces, or a burst of listing actions across unrelated services in a short window.

beginner.definition: Cloud platforms keep their own lists of groups, roles and permissions. A role is a named bundle of allowed actions. This technique is an attacker reading those lists through the cloud interface. It is the cloud version of the parent technique, Permission Groups Discovery.
beginner.whyItMatters: In the cloud, permissions do the work that locked doors do in an office. Reading the lists shows exactly which accounts can change or delete things. A single read only call can reveal a great deal. Since automation makes similar calls all the time, this activity is easy to miss.
howItWorks: The attacker signs in to the cloud platform with a stolen key or session.
They ask the platform which roles exist and who belongs to them.
They ask which groups one particular user account is a member of.
In AWS they list the policies attached to a role to see what it may do.
They may also read the access list of a stored file to find other permitted accounts.
The results point them at the accounts and services worth attacking next.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel where every door opens with a key card. The front desk keeps a printed list of who may enter which floor. A thief does not need to break a door. He only has to stand near the desk and read the list. Then he follows the guest who can open the manager's office. In the cloud, permissions are the doors, the list is the identity interface, and reading it costs nothing.
takeaways: In the cloud, identity permissions are the real doors to protect.
Turn on audit logging so every listing call records who asked.
Compare new enumeration callers against your known automation identities.

objectives: Explain what cloud roles, groups and policies represent.
Describe the interface calls used to enumerate cloud groups and permissions.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from its parent, Permission Groups Discovery.
Identify the audit log fields that attribute an enumeration call to an identity.
Explain why routine cloud automation makes this activity hard to detect.
